teaching_blocks.title: The situation
teaching_blocks.content: Imagine opening a supplied mobile app, making the supplied source edit, and finding that the running screen still looks unchanged. There are two questions to separate: did you send the change to the app, and did the changed code execute again? Running and iterating means connecting an edit to an observable result on the supplied target, not merely saving the file.

teaching_blocks.title: The working contract
teaching_blocks.content: Run a supplied project with `flutter run` on a physical or virtual target in debug mode to use hot reload. After modifying a Dart source file, enter `r` in the running terminal or use the editor's hot-reload control and check the running app for the change. Hot reload preserves application state, whereas hot restart restarts the Flutter app and loses that state. A source change becomes visible only if the changed code executes again; use restart when the change requires application initialization to run again.

teaching_blocks.title: Trace the relationships
teaching_blocks.content: Follow the running example through both actions. With hot reload, ask what the screen should show given that its current application state is preserved. With hot restart, ask what should show after application initialization runs again and the earlier state is lost. Those are different expected results even when both actions use the same edited source. This comparison explains why you should choose an action from the changed code's need to execute again, rather than assuming that the most convenient action proves the edit. The final evidence is the intended change in the running app, not just an action taken in the terminal.

teaching_blocks.title: Apply it to the supplied feature
teaching_blocks.content: Start the supplied project with `flutter run` on the provided physical or virtual target in debug mode. Make the exercise's Dart edit, then enter `r` in the running terminal or use the editor's hot-reload control. Compare the intended change with the running app. Suppose the exercise has already put the app into a particular state: hot reload keeps that state, so you can check the edit without treating this as a fresh application start. If the edit affects initialization that must run again, use restart and check the result after initialization instead.

teaching_blocks.title: Keep the distinction clear
teaching_blocks.content: Hot reload is not a promise that every edit immediately appears. A changed section must execute again. Hot restart is not state-preserving reload under another name: it restarts the Flutter app and loses its current state.

teaching_blocks.title: Check the result
teaching_blocks.content: Separate the evidence you collect: the project is running in debug mode, the reload action was sent, and the expected source change is visible. If visibility is missing, ask whether the changed code has executed again before assuming that saving or reloading failed. Choose the restart action when initialization is the part that needs to run again.

teaching_blocks.title: The situation
teaching_blocks.content: A supplied function keeps track of an order count and a fixed delivery label. The count changes as the function works, but the label should keep its first value. A declaration gives a value a name and establishes the type and reassignment rules that later statements must respect.

teaching_blocks.title: The working contract
teaching_blocks.content: `var name = value;` infers the variable's type from its initializer; an explicit declaration uses `Type name = value;`. An ordinary variable can be reassigned with `name = value;`, subject to its declared or inferred type. `final` permits a variable to be assigned once; `const` declares a compile-time constant and is implicitly final. Use `final` for a value that will not be reassigned and `var` for a local value that must be reassigned.

teaching_blocks.title: Trace the relationships
teaching_blocks.content: Trace the count declaration as a contract that continues after its first line. Its initializer establishes the inferred type, and its later assignment must remain within that type. Trace the label differently: the final modifier permits its one assignment but not a later replacement of that variable's value. For a const declaration, additionally ask whether the value is a compile-time constant. These questions let you explain the modifier choice in the supplied function: the count needs reassignment, the label does not, and a compile-time value has the additional const property. The declaration and the function's later statements should tell the same story.

teaching_blocks.title: Apply it to the supplied feature
teaching_blocks.content: For a changing count, `var orderCount = 2;` infers a type from the integer initializer. At this point orderCount is 2. After `orderCount = 3;`, it is 3: the reassignment stays within its inferred type. `int orderCount = 2;` is the explicit-type alternative, not a second declaration to place beside the first. Contrast `final deliveryLabel = 'Ready';`: this example assigns the label once and does not reassign it; a later replacement is not permitted. A compile-time value can instead be declared with `const`. Choose the modifier according to whether this variable will receive another assignment.

teaching_blocks.title: Keep the distinction clear
teaching_blocks.content: `var` does not mean that later assignments can use any type. Inference establishes a type from the initializer. Also distinguish a final variable from a compile-time constant: both restrict assignment, but only `const` makes the declaration a compile-time constant.

teaching_blocks.title: Check the result
teaching_blocks.content: Read the supplied function before choosing the modifier. Identify the first value, determine whether another assignment is needed, and compare every later assigned value with the variable's type. Check a changing variable and a non-reassigned variable separately. This makes the declaration an intentional part of the function's behavior rather than a modifier chosen by habit.

teaching_blocks.title: The situation
teaching_blocks.content: You edit a supplied Dart declaration and the analyzer reports a source problem. The diagnostic is a precise starting point: it has a name, a message, and a location. Correcting it means connecting that report to the indicated statement and then checking the result with analysis again.

teaching_blocks.title: The working contract
teaching_blocks.content: Analyzer diagnostics identify source problems with a diagnostic name, message, and source location. Use the diagnostic's description and documented correction to edit the indicated source, then run `flutter analyze` again to check the correction.

teaching_blocks.title: Trace the relationships
teaching_blocks.content: The loop has two reports, with the source edit between them. The first report tells you what problem to investigate and where; the second tells you whether your documented correction addressed it. Keep those roles separate. For the supplied reassignment diagnostic, the useful reasoning is the connection between the message, the indicated statement, and the documented correction—not the number of lines changed. If reanalysis still reports the problem, the same three pieces of evidence remain the starting point. A clean result for that diagnostic closes this particular correction loop without requiring unrelated changes elsewhere.

teaching_blocks.title: Apply it to the supplied feature
teaching_blocks.content: Suppose the exercise supplies a diagnostic about one reassignment. Read its name and message, go to its source location, and compare the indicated declaration and assignment with the diagnostic's documented correction. Make that correction at the identified source, then run `flutter analyze`. The useful result is a new analysis report showing whether that particular problem remains. Keep the example focused on the supplied diagnostic rather than making unrelated edits elsewhere in the project.

teaching_blocks.title: Keep the distinction clear
teaching_blocks.content: Changing a nearby line is not itself evidence that the diagnostic is fixed. The verification step is reanalysis. Likewise, the source location identifies the reported problem; it is not an instruction to rewrite the whole surrounding file.

teaching_blocks.title: Check the result
teaching_blocks.content: Use a small evidence trail: retain the original diagnostic name, note the source location you edited, and compare the new report with the original one. If the same problem remains, return to its description and correction. This teaches a repeatable diagnostic-to-source loop without introducing general debugging or editor setup as new Flutter topics.

teaching_blocks.title: The situation
teaching_blocks.content: A mobile order screen needs an eligibility result from supplied values. You might need to compare a total with a limit and combine that comparison with another boolean condition. An expression describes how values are calculated or tested; its grouping matters as much as the individual operators.

teaching_blocks.title: The working contract
teaching_blocks.content: Arithmetic operators `+`, `-`, `*`, `/`, `~/`, and `%` mean addition, subtraction, multiplication, division, integer division, and remainder respectively. Comparisons `==`, `!=`, `<`, `>`, `<=`, and `>=` produce boolean results for equality, inequality, and ordering tests. Combine boolean conditions using `&&` for conjunction, `||` for disjunction, and `!` for negation. Operator precedence determines expression grouping; parentheses explicitly choose the grouping.

teaching_blocks.title: Trace the relationships
teaching_blocks.content: Separate the eligibility expression into questions in the same order as its intended grouping. The amount comparison asks whether the amount meets the limit. The delivery boolean supplies another true-or-false input. Conjunction requires both; disjunction represents an alternative; negation reverses a boolean condition. Before combining them, write the intended decision in plain language so an alternative is not accidentally treated as a requirement. Parentheses then record the grouping you chose. The numerical division examples are a reminder that an operator expresses a specific operation, not just a general instruction to calculate something with two values.

teaching_blocks.title: Apply it to the supplied feature
teaching_blocks.content: Take an illustrative eligibility rule: the amount is at least 20 and delivery is enabled. With `amount = 24` and `deliveryEnabled = true`, `amount >= 20 && deliveryEnabled` gives true; with amount 18 it gives false. For arithmetic, trace the same inputs through three different operations: `5 / 2 = 2.5` is division, retaining the fractional part; `5 ~/ 2 = 2` is integer division, giving the whole-number quotient; `5 % 2 = 1` is remainder, because two groups of 2 use 4 of the 5, leaving 1. The remainder is not the quotient or its fractional part. These are separate illustrative expressions. When an eligibility rule combines alternatives and requirements, parentheses record the intended grouping.

teaching_blocks.title: Keep the distinction clear
teaching_blocks.content: The symbol `=` used for assignment is not the equality comparison `==`. Also, division, integer division, and remainder answer different questions. An expression can contain the right values but still produce the wrong eligibility result if its logical groups do not match the requirement.

teaching_blocks.title: Check the result
teaching_blocks.content: Trace one supplied input at a time: compute the arithmetic parts, evaluate the comparisons, then combine the boolean results with the intended grouping. Include a case that should be eligible and a case that should not. State the expected result before evaluating the expression, so you are checking the requirement rather than accepting whichever result the expression happens to produce.

teaching_blocks.title: The situation
teaching_blocks.content: An order card needs a label containing a supplied order number. A string literal provides the fixed text, and interpolation places the changing value inside that text without changing the label's intended wording.

teaching_blocks.title: The working contract
teaching_blocks.content: Use single or double quotes to write a string literal. Write `$identifier` to interpolate a variable or `${expression}` to interpolate a more complex expression in a string. Interpolation obtains an object's string representation by calling its `toString()` method. Use a backslash to escape a matching quote within a quoted string.

teaching_blocks.title: Apply it to the supplied feature

If the label includes an expression rather than just a variable name, braces mark the expression: with `count` equal to 2, `'Items: ${count + 1}'` produces `Items: 3`. Use single or double quotes consistently, and escape a matching quote with a backslash when it occurs inside the literal. Interpolation uses the interpolated object's string representation; it is not a separate model-formatting rule.

teaching_blocks.title: Keep the distinction clear
teaching_blocks.content: The braces in `${expression}` are significant. `$identifier` is for a variable name, not a whole arithmetic expression. Also do not assume interpolation chooses a special business display format: it obtains the object's representation through `toString()`.

teaching_blocks.title: Keep the scope focused
teaching_blocks.content: Check the exact output characters against the supplied label requirement, including punctuation and spaces.

teaching_blocks.title: The situation
teaching_blocks.content: An order calculation should produce a result from a clear set of inputs. A function packages that calculation behind parameters and a return type. The caller must know which inputs bind by position, which bind by name, and which can be omitted.

teaching_blocks.title: The working contract
teaching_blocks.content: Define a function with typed parameters and a return type, using `return expression;` in its body to produce a result. Required positional arguments bind in parameter order and must be supplied by the caller. Parameters inside `{...}` are named and are passed with `parameterName: value`; mark a named parameter `required` when callers must provide it. Parameters inside `[...]` are optional positional parameters; use `= constantValue` to supply a default when the caller omits an optional parameter. An arrow body `=> expression;` is shorthand for returning that expression.

teaching_blocks.title: Trace the relationships
teaching_blocks.content: The declaration is the caller's binding contract. Look at the parameter section before following the body: positional parameters answer which argument comes first or next, named parameters answer which label identifies the argument, and defaults answer what is used if an optional argument is omitted. Then follow the bound values to the returned result. A wrong result may come from binding the right values to the wrong positional parameters rather than from arithmetic inside the function. In the named case, check the parameter name and required marker independently. These checks keep calling rules separate from the computation they feed.

teaching_blocks.title: Apply it to the supplied feature
Keep the distinction clear
teaching_blocks.content: An optional parameter is not the same thing as a required named parameter. Naming improves explicit binding but does not, by itself, make the input mandatory. An arrow body returns one expression; it is not a substitute for an arbitrary multi-statement function body.

teaching_blocks.title: Check the result
teaching_blocks.content: For the supplied function, pair every call argument with its parameter and record the value that parameter receives. Include one call using all required inputs and one that omits an optional input. Follow the body to its returned expression and verify the expected result. Keep the implementation to the specified input contract rather than adding unrelated overload-like alternatives.

teaching_blocks.title: The situation
teaching_blocks.content: An order model needs a stable identity and a display label each time a new order instance is created. A class defines the instance fields, and its constructor establishes the required field values. This makes the constructor the place to check whether the model starts with the data its callers expect.

teaching_blocks.title: The working contract
teaching_blocks.content: Declare an instance's typed fields inside a class and access an instance member with `instance.member`. A generative constructor has the class's name and initializes a newly created instance. Use initializing formal parameters such as `ClassName(this.field);` or `ClassName({required this.field});` to assign arguments to instance fields. Initialize final instance fields at declaration, with initializing formal parameters, or in an initializer list before the constructor body runs. A `final` instance field is assigned once and cannot subsequently be reassigned.

teaching_blocks.title: Trace the relationships
teaching_blocks.content: Think of the constructor as the transition from supplied arguments to an initialized instance. In the Order example, pair each argument with the final field it establishes and then read that field through the created instance. If the initializing formals are named, use their names for the pairing; if positional, use their positions. A final field's once-assigned rule remains in effect after construction. The important difference from an ordinary changing local variable is that the instance field cannot later be reassigned. Keep every required field's initialization visible rather than expecting the constructor body to repair a missing final-field initialization afterward.

teaching_blocks.title: Apply it to the supplied feature
Keep the distinction clear
teaching_blocks.content: Declaring a final instance field does not make its initialization optional. Establish it at declaration, through an initializing formal, or in an initializer list before the constructor body. Also, a class name and an instance member play different roles: the constructor creates an instance; member access uses that instance.

teaching_blocks.title: Check the result
teaching_blocks.content: List the model's required fields, find where each receives its initial value, and trace one constructor call through those assignments. Read the resulting instance members and compare them with the supplied model requirement. This gives a concrete check of the model's starting state without extending the lesson into inheritance, serialization, or database mapping.

teaching_blocks.title: The situation
teaching_blocks.content: A supplied screen has a heading and a body section. In Flutter you describe that structure with widgets rather than editing an existing widget object to change what it says. Think of the widget tree as the current UI description, made from configurations passed into other widgets.

teaching_blocks.title: The working contract
teaching_blocks.content: Widgets are immutable descriptions of part of a user interface, with their configuration held in final fields. Compose a widget tree by passing another widget to a `child` argument or a list of widgets to `children`, according to the receiving widget's API. To change a widget's configuration, create a new widget configuration rather than mutate the existing widget.

teaching_blocks.title: Trace the relationships
teaching_blocks.content: Read the composition from both sides of each connection. The outer widget API says whether it accepts one child or a children list; the nested configuration supplies the widget or widgets that fill that role. This is why you should not infer the argument name solely from how many visual parts you see. In the changed-heading case, the old configuration still describes its old input and the new configuration describes the changed one. That separates immutable descriptions from the ordinary fact that an interface can have different descriptions over time. First check structure, then compare the input values in each description.

teaching_blocks.title: Apply it to the supplied feature
teaching_blocks.content: For the supplied structure, identify which receiving API expects a single `child` and which expects a list called `children`. Put the body widget into a single-child slot when that API requests one widget; use the children list when the container accepts several. Suppose the heading input changes from one supplied label to another. Create a new widget configuration containing the new value rather than assigning over a final field of the earlier widget. The composition exercise is about matching the described UI structure, not yet about how a particular layout allocates space.

teaching_blocks.title: Keep the distinction clear
teaching_blocks.content: Immutable does not mean the screen can never change. It means the existing widget configuration is not mutated; a changed description is represented by a new configuration. Also, `child` and `children` are receiving-API choices, not interchangeable argument spellings.

teaching_blocks.title: Check the result
teaching_blocks.content: Trace the supplied tree from the outer widget to its leaves. At each connection, check whether the receiving constructor expects one child or a collection. Compare the completed description with the required heading/body structure. For a changed input, point to the new configuration that represents it and leave the old configuration unchanged.

teaching_blocks.title: The situation
teaching_blocks.content: An order summary receives its current label as configuration and should describe a subtree from that input. A StatelessWidget is useful here because the teaching target is deriving UI from current configuration and context, not storing a changing local value inside the view.

teaching_blocks.title: The working contract
teaching_blocks.content: A StatelessWidget describes UI using its configuration and the BuildContext passed to its build method. Implement `Widget build(BuildContext context)` to return the widget subtree derived from those inputs. The framework may call build after insertion, a configuration change, or a change to an inherited dependency; do not rely on build running only once. The build method should have no side effects beyond building a widget.

teaching_blocks.title: Trace the relationships
teaching_blocks.content: Repeatability is the important property to check in this build method. If the configuration says Ready, the returned subtree should describe Ready. If a later configuration says Dispatched, derive the description from that later input rather than assuming the earlier build was the only one. The framework can also call build because an inherited dependency changed. Treat the supplied context as part of the input relationship, not merely a parameter that is always irrelevant. By keeping the method free of side effects beyond widget building, you avoid assigning a one-time operation to a method the framework may call repeatedly.

teaching_blocks.title: Apply it to the supplied feature
teaching_blocks.content: In the supplied stateless view, implement `Widget build(BuildContext context)` and return the subtree described by the current inputs. Imagine receiving the label Ready first and Dispatched in a later configuration. Each build should derive the output from the configuration it receives, so the second description uses Dispatched. Keep actions such as starting an operation out of this method: the method's job is building a widget. Its context is also an input, so a relevant inherited dependency change can lead the framework to call build again.

teaching_blocks.title: Keep the distinction clear
teaching_blocks.content: Stateless does not mean build runs once. The framework may call it after insertion, configuration changes, or inherited-dependency changes. If the method assumes a single call, that assumption conflicts with its role as a repeatable description of the current UI.

teaching_blocks.title: Check the result
teaching_blocks.content: Review the method as a mapping from inputs to subtree. Check one configuration, then a changed configuration, and ask whether both produce the required description. Check that the method does not perform side effects beyond building widgets. Leave owner-managed mutable state and asynchronous work to their own lessons rather than trying to fit them into this stateless view.

teaching_blocks.title: The situation
teaching_blocks.content: A supplied card overflows its available width. Before changing arbitrary widths, separate what the parent permits from what the child requests. Flutter layout passes constraints down, receives chosen sizes back, and then positions children; a child cannot treat its preferred size as the only input.

teaching_blocks.title: The working contract
teaching_blocks.content: A parent passes constraints down, children pass chosen sizes up, and parents position their children. Constraints specify minimum and maximum width and height, and a child chooses a size within those limits. For an overflow, inspect the parent's constraints and the child's requested size to identify which dimension cannot fit. Bound a child with `ConstrainedBox(constraints: const BoxConstraints(minWidth: 70, minHeight: 70, maxWidth: 150, maxHeight: 150), child: child)`; these are additional bounds within the parent constraints, not replacements for them: with a parent permitting that range an oversized child is limited to 150, but tight parent constraints can force a size outside the requested range.

teaching_blocks.title: Trace the relationships
teaching_blocks.content: Keep four measurements separate: the parent's minimum, the parent's maximum, the child's requested size, and the child's chosen size. The constraint interval determines which chosen sizes are permitted. A requested size outside that interval does not become valid just because the child wants it. The ConstrainedBox adds bounds within that relationship; it does not remove the parent's limits. This makes the two supplied parent cases genuinely different: a parent permitting the example's range allows the 150 limit, while tight parent constraints can force a size outside the added requested range. Follow the real incoming constraints before interpreting the bound.

teaching_blocks.title: Apply it to the supplied feature
teaching_blocks.content: Suppose the parent allows the range in the brief's ConstrainedBox example. The additional bounds request a minimum of 70 and maximum of 150 in each dimension, so an oversized child is limited to 150 in that setting. Now change the scenario: the parent has tight constraints that force a size outside that requested range. The ConstrainedBox bounds do not replace those parent constraints. In the overflow exercise, inspect the actual parent's minimum and maximum width and height, then compare the child's requested size. Identify the dimension that cannot fit before selecting the supplied repair.

teaching_blocks.title: Keep the distinction clear
teaching_blocks.content: Adding a ConstrainedBox is not permission to override the parent. The resulting size depends on the incoming constraints as well as the added bounds. Also, an overflow symptom does not tell you by itself whether width or height is the dimension causing the problem.

teaching_blocks.title: Check the result
teaching_blocks.content: Draw a small parent-to-child trace with the actual constraints, the requested size, and the size the child can choose within the applicable limits. Compare the screen after the bounded repair with the requirement. Keep the explanation on this local constraint relationship rather than introducing scrolling or flex as universal solutions to every overflow.

teaching_blocks.title: The situation
teaching_blocks.content: A supplied order section needs its label and amount placed along a horizontal line, while another section stacks fields vertically. Row and Column choose the primary direction; alignment then positions children along that direction and across it.

teaching_blocks.title: The working contract
teaching_blocks.content: Row arranges its children horizontally; Column arranges its children vertically. Set `mainAxisAlignment` to position children along the primary axis and `crossAxisAlignment` along the perpendicular axis. `start`, `end`, and `center` select alignment within an axis, while main-axis `spaceBetween`, `spaceAround`, and `spaceEvenly` distribute free space. For a Row, horizontal start depends on text direction; for a Column, vertical start depends on vertical direction.

teaching_blocks.title: Apply it to the supplied feature
teaching_blocks.content: For a Row, reason about horizontal placement as main-axis placement and vertical placement as cross-axis placement. For a Column, swap those roles. If the requirement is equal gaps between neighboring items, compare it with main-axis `spaceBetween`; if it calls for spacing around items or evenly distributed gaps, compare `spaceAround` and `spaceEvenly`. Use start, end, or center when the intended placement is alignment rather than free-space distribution. Interpret a Row's horizontal start using text direction and a Column's vertical start using vertical direction.

teaching_blocks.title: Keep the distinction clear

teaching_blocks.title: The situation
teaching_blocks.content: A supplied order model may have no delivery note. Nullable typing makes that absence explicit: the code should handle a missing value before using it as present. The goal is not to silence a type warning, but to choose the behavior the feature requires when the value is absent.

teaching_blocks.title: The working contract
teaching_blocks.content: Append `?` to a type to allow null; an ordinary non-nullable type excludes null. Guard a local nullable variable with a null check before using it as non-null, allowing flow analysis to promote it where applicable. Use `value ?? fallback` to substitute a fallback when the value is null. Use `?.` to access a member only when the receiver is not null. The postfix `!` asserts that a value is not null; if it is null the assertion fails at runtime, so handle an uncertain nullable value with a check instead.

teaching_blocks.title: Trace the relationships
teaching_blocks.content: Follow the absent note without pretending it is a present string. The nullable type allows that absence; the chosen null-handling operation determines the next behavior. A check can establish presence for a local value where promotion applies, a fallback chooses another value for null, and conditional access avoids a member access when the receiver is null. An assertion instead claims that null is impossible at that point. These are different claims about the same input. In the supplied present and absent cases, state which claim is justified before choosing the operator, rather than treating all null-related operators as interchangeable conveniences.

teaching_blocks.title: Apply it to the supplied feature

If the required absent-note label is No note, `note ?? 'No note'` supplies that fallback only when note is null. A member access with `?.` runs only for a non-null receiver. Compare a present note with a null note: the first retains its text, while the second uses the specified absence behavior. Do not insert `!` simply because the present-note case worked.

teaching_blocks.title: Keep the distinction clear
teaching_blocks.content: The postfix `!` is an assertion, not a check or a fallback. If the asserted value is null, the assertion fails at runtime. Also, promotion from a null check is subject to flow analysis; the brief does not promise that every nullable expression is promoted in every context.

teaching_blocks.title: The situation
teaching_blocks.content: An order feature needs an ordered sequence of items, a collection of unique tags, and values found by an identity key. List, Set, and Map provide different collection relationships, with type arguments describing the elements or key/value pairs each accepts.

teaching_blocks.title: The working contract
teaching_blocks.content: A `List<T>` is an ordered collection with elements constrained to T; create a typed literal with `<T>[...]` and access elements using zero-based indexing. A `Set<T>` stores unique elements; create one with `<T>{...}` and add elements using `add`. A `Map<K, V>` associates unique keys with values; create `<K, V>{key: value}`, write with `map[key] = value`, and read with `map[key]`. A map lookup can return null when its key is absent, even when its value type is non-nullable. Adding an incompatible type to a typed collection is an error rather than an automatic conversion to the element type.

teaching_blocks.title: Trace the relationships
teaching_blocks.content: Trace each collection using the relationship it promises. The list's first and second items have indexes 0 and 1, so an index is a position rather than an arbitrary key. The set's repeated tag is still a unique element, so it does not behave as a tally of every addition. The map associates a key with a value; a missing key can yield null even though stored values have a non-nullable declared type. In each case, the type arguments constrain what can be inserted. Keep those relationship and type questions separate when checking which supplied operations are valid.

teaching_blocks.title: Apply it to the supplied feature
teaching_blocks.content: An illustrative `<String>['Tea', 'Bread']` list has Tea at index 0 and Bread at index 1. Read it through the key and handle a missing key with a null check or the intended fallback. These examples represent separate data needs, not three interchangeable ways to model the same behavior.

teaching_blocks.title: Keep the distinction clear
teaching_blocks.content: A map whose value type is non-nullable can still return null for an absent key. Also, a typed collection does not automatically convert an incompatible value into the declared element type. Decide which collection relationship is needed before choosing its literal syntax.

teaching_blocks.title: The situation
teaching_blocks.content: A supplied stateful section owns a resource that must survive ordinary rebuilds but must be released when its owner ends. teaching_blocks.title: The situation
teaching_blocks.content: A supplied model exists, but a consumer cannot resolve it from its context. Provider lookup is a tree-scope question: the provider must be above the consumer, and the lookup context must be below the provider that exposes the value.

teaching_blocks.title: The working contract
teaching_blocks.content: Place a provider as an ancestor of all widgets that need the provided value. A lookup using BuildContext returns the nearest matching provider of the requested type. teaching_blocks.title: Trace the relationships

The nearest matching provider is the value the lookup resolves. The new provider cannot serve a context above itself, even if the source code for the two is nearby. In the supplied existing-model example, Provider.value exposes that instance to the child subtree. Check both the placement of the value and the placement of each consumer's context. teaching_blocks.title: Apply it to the supplied feature

If another matching provider is nearer to a particular consumer, that nearer provider is the relevant match. Draw the lookup context beside the consumer rather than treating every context in the screen as equivalent.

teaching_blocks.title: Keep the distinction clear

teaching_blocks.title: The situation

teaching_blocks.title: The working contract

teaching_blocks.title: The situation
teaching_blocks.content: A supplied shared model needs a clear owner. Creating a new notifier for a provider and exposing a model already owned elsewhere are different lifetime decisions. Choose the provider constructor that matches that ownership instead of treating create and value as stylistic alternatives.

teaching_blocks.title: The working contract
teaching_blocks.content: Use `ChangeNotifierProvider(create: (_) => Model(), child: ...)` for a newly created model that the provider owns. ChangeNotifierProvider automatically disposes a model it creates when that provider leaves the tree. Use `ChangeNotifierProvider.value(value: existingModel, child: ...)` to expose an already-owned model rather than transfer its ownership through create.

teaching_blocks.title: Trace the relationships
teaching_blocks.content: Begin with the model's origin. If create constructs it for this ChangeNotifierProvider, the provider owns that new model and disposes it when leaving the tree. If the supplied model already has an owner, value exposes that existing model. The constructor choice communicates a lifetime relationship rather than an incidental syntax preference. In the ownership diagram, keep the owner of the existing model visible instead of assuming that exposing it transfers creation responsibility. Use that distinction when comparing the two snippets, and do not combine them into a single pattern that treats every passed model as newly provider-owned.

teaching_blocks.title: Apply it to the supplied feature
teaching_blocks.content: For a newly created model, use `ChangeNotifierProvider(create: (_) => Model(), child: ...)`. That provider owns the notifier it creates and automatically disposes it when the provider leaves the tree. For an existing model supplied by another owner, use `ChangeNotifierProvider.value(value: existingModel, child: ...)`. In the second case, you are exposing an already-owned instance, not transferring it through create. Trace where the model first comes from before choosing the constructor.

teaching_blocks.title: Keep the distinction clear

teaching_blocks.title: The situation
teaching_blocks.content: A supplied view renders order data but its event handler also performs source-specific work. The recommended architecture separates those responsibilities: the view renders and forwards events, while UI and data layers carry the state, orchestration, and external access responsibilities.

teaching_blocks.title: The working contract
teaching_blocks.content: In the recommended architecture, a view renders data and forwards interaction events rather than implement business or data-source logic. Keep application state and action orchestration in the UI layer, exposing the values and callbacks that the view needs. Place source-specific external access in the data layer and call it through the existing layer boundary rather than put that access in the view. Refactor an event handler to call a command while keeping its input and observable outcome unchanged, rather than make the view perform the data operation itself.

teaching_blocks.title: Trace the relationships
teaching_blocks.content: Follow one interaction through the supplied boundaries. The view forwards its input to the command; application logic orchestrates the action and exposes the state the view renders; source-specific work stays in the data layer. The refactor succeeds when these responsibility locations change as intended while the input and observable outcome remain the same. This is a recommended architectural division, so preserve that scope instead of calling it the only valid Flutter structure. The most useful before/after comparison is the same event and result, with the source operation no longer implemented by the view's event handler.

teaching_blocks.title: Apply it to the supplied feature

Keep application state and action orchestration in the UI layer, exposing the values and callbacks the view needs. Place source-specific access in the data layer behind the existing boundary. teaching_blocks.title: The situation
teaching_blocks.content: A supplied Material screen works in the app but a widget test must construct the environment it depends on. The harness is the test's widget tree, including required ancestors and model dependencies, not just the screen placed in isolation.

teaching_blocks.title: The working contract

teaching_blocks.title: Trace the relationships

For each dependency the test screen needs, identify the ancestor or model value that the harness actually supplies. PumpWidget builds and renders that test tree; it does not implicitly borrow missing ancestors from another tree. The supplied Material screen therefore needs its relevant MaterialApp environment in the harness, and its lookups need models placed above it. Keep the initial rendering check focused on this construction. Later finder and interaction assertions will have a meaningful screen to inspect because this environment is explicit.

teaching_blocks.title: The situation
teaching_blocks.content: A supplied widget test needs to prove that a particular label or keyed control exists after the tree is built. A finder describes what to locate, and an expectation states how many matches are acceptable. These are separate parts of a precise UI assertion.

teaching_blocks.title: The working contract
teaching_blocks.content: Use `find.text('text')` to locate Text widgets displaying a given string. Use `find.byKey(key)` for a keyed widget or `find.byType(Type)` to locate widgets of a type. Assert a finder result with `expect(finder, findsOneWidget)` for one match or `findsNothing` for no match. Create the widget tree before evaluating a finder-based assertion.

teaching_blocks.title: Trace the relationships
teaching_blocks.content: The test assertion has three components: a built tree, a finder targeting the requirement, and a match-count expectation. In the Saved-label case, text defines the target and findsOneWidget defines the acceptable count. A key or type target uses its corresponding finder instead. FindsNothing is a deliberate absence expectation, not simply an assertion that something else exists. Trace these pieces in order so a test failure can be interpreted against the stated visible requirement. Do not treat the presence of any widget of a broad type as automatically proving a more specific label or keyed-control requirement.

teaching_blocks.title: Apply it to the supplied feature
teaching_blocks.content:
After creating the supplied widget tree, assert the illustrative Saved label with:
```dart
expect(find.text('Saved'), findsOneWidget);
```
`find.text('Saved')` targets Text widgets displaying Saved; findsOneWidget requires exactly one match. The assertion passes with one matching widget and fails with zero or more than one. To assert absence instead, use findsNothing. If the requirement identifies a keyed control, use find.byKey(key); if it identifies a widget type, use find.byType(Type). Choose the finder and expected count from the acceptance target, not whichever query happens to return something.

teaching_blocks.title: Keep the distinction clear
teaching_blocks.content: A finder is not itself an assertion that the required widget exists. The match expectation makes that claim testable. Also, evaluate finder-based assertions after constructing the tree; an unbuilt tree is not evidence about the supplied screen's intended content.

teaching_blocks.title: Check the result
teaching_blocks.content: Write the expected visible result first, choose text, key, or type to identify it, and state the required match count. teaching_blocks.title: The situation
teaching_blocks.content: A supplied operation can fail with a known exception, and the feature needs a distinct failure outcome. Exception handling connects that raised failure to an appropriate handler instead of letting successful-path statements stand in for a result that was never produced.

teaching_blocks.title: The working contract
teaching_blocks.content: `throw` raises an exception and execution unwinds until a matching handler is found. Handle a known exception type with `try { ... } on ExpectedType catch (e) { ... }` rather than catch all failures indiscriminately. Use `catch (e, stackTrace)` when the handler needs both the exception and its trace. Use `rethrow` when a caught failure must propagate to another handler instead of be swallowed.

teaching_blocks.title: Trace the relationships
teaching_blocks.content: The success trace and failure trace leave the try block differently. A normal result permits its dependent successful path; a throw unwinds toward a matching handler. At that handler, decide from the supplied boundary contract whether to produce a failure outcome or rethrow to another handler. The known exception type makes that decision specific. If the trace is needed, the second catch parameter provides it. Keep caught-failure handling distinct from success: suppressing a failure without the required translation or propagation does not establish the successful result that the operation would have returned.

teaching_blocks.title: Apply it to the supplied feature
teaching_blocks.content: Place the supplied operation in a try block and use `on ExpectedType catch (e)` for its documented failure type. When that exception is thrown, execution unwinds until a matching handler is found; trace the handler rather than continuing as though the operation returned normally. If the supplied reporting contract needs the trace as well as the exception, use `catch (e, stackTrace)`. If another boundary must handle the caught failure, use rethrow so the failure propagates instead of being swallowed.

teaching_blocks.title: Keep the distinction clear
teaching_blocks.content: Catching a failure is not the same as resolving it successfully. A handler that suppresses a failure changes its propagation. Prefer the known exception type over indiscriminate handling that treats every failure as the same expected outcome.

teaching_blocks.title: Check the result
teaching_blocks.content: For the supplied success and failure cases, identify which statements execute and which handler matches. Check whether the boundary should translate the failure or propagate it further. Keep this lesson about Dart exception control flow rather than inventing a retry policy or a new error-reporting service.

teaching_blocks.title: The situation
teaching_blocks.content: A supplied Flutter callback fails and the report contains both framework and application frames. The reporting frame tells you how the error was surfaced; it is not necessarily the application statement that caused the failure. Read the report before selecting a source location to inspect.

teaching_blocks.title: The working contract
teaching_blocks.content: Flutter catches errors from framework callbacks and reports them through FlutterError.onError; the default handler presents them in device logs. Read the reported exception and framework context, then inspect the call stack to locate the application call that caused the failure. Select the first relevant application frame and inspect that frame's source and variables rather than treat a framework reporting frame as the faulty application statement.

teaching_blocks.title: Trace the relationships
teaching_blocks.content: Use the report's parts as a sequence of evidence. The exception says what was reported, the framework context describes where it was surfaced, and the stack helps locate the relevant application call. The first relevant application frame gives the source and variables to inspect. This is different from assuming the top framework reporting frame is the defective statement. In the supplied callback failure, connect the observed exception with the chosen application source so the report explains a concrete call rather than prompting a broad rewrite. Keep FlutterError.onError's reporting role distinct from the source of the application failure.

teaching_blocks.title: Apply it to the supplied feature
teaching_blocks.content: Start with the reported exception and framework context, then inspect its call stack. Flutter catches framework-callback errors and reports them through FlutterError.onError; the default handler presents them in device logs. In the supplied stack, select the first relevant application frame and inspect that frame's source and variables. teaching_blocks.title: The situation

teaching_blocks.title: The situation
teaching_blocks.content: A supplied feature needs permission before accessing a mobile capability. Read the current status and request authorization when the feature needs it; then decide from the returned status whether the action can proceed.

teaching_blocks.title: The working contract
teaching_blocks.content: Read a capability's current status with `await Permission.capability.status`. Call `await Permission.capability.request()` when the feature needs authorization and use the returned status to decide whether to proceed. A request returns the new permission status; if permission was already granted, requesting it again does not display another authorization dialog. Limit permission requests to access relevant to the requested feature and respect the user's decision.

teaching_blocks.title: Trace the relationships
teaching_blocks.content: The permission trace has an intent, a status, a request when needed, and a result-dependent action. The supplied feature determines why authorization is relevant; the returned status determines whether that feature can proceed. Requesting an already-granted permission produces its status without displaying another authorization dialog. This prevents the example from teaching a dialog as the mandatory observable result of every request call. Keep the user's decision in the branch outcome, and keep the request limited to feature-relevant access. Use the contract's non-proceeding behavior when authorization is not granted rather than treating the request call itself as permission.

teaching_blocks.title: Apply it to the supplied feature
teaching_blocks.content: Use `await Permission.capability.status` with the supplied capability in place of the placeholder. Limit requests to access relevant to the requested feature and respect the user's choice.

teaching_blocks.title: Keep the distinction clear

teaching_blocks.title: The situation
teaching_blocks.content: A supplied permission request does not grant access, and the feature needs a respectful fallback. Denied, restricted, and permanentlyDenied have different meanings, so read the right status source before deciding whether another prompt or settings action is appropriate.

teaching_blocks.title: The working contract
teaching_blocks.content: A denied status can mean permission was not requested or was denied before; restricted means the operating system limits access, such as through parental controls. A permanentlyDenied request result means the user must change permission in system settings rather than receive another prompt. Branch on the request result and provide an unavailable-feature fallback for denied or restricted access rather than continue as if access were granted. Offer `openAppSettings()` for an appropriate permanently denied case instead of repeatedly presenting a permission prompt. On Android, the status getter reports denied even for permanent denial, so use the request result when distinguishing permanent denial.

teaching_blocks.title: Trace the relationships
teaching_blocks.content: Keep the source of each status beside its meaning. A request result can identify permanentlyDenied, which calls for a settings change rather than another prompt. Android's status getter still reports denied for permanent denial, so a getter-only trace cannot establish that distinction. Restricted is an operating-system limitation, not the same description as a user denial. For denied or restricted access, the supplied unavailable-feature fallback is the outcome rather than the protected action. When settings is appropriate for permanent denial, offer it deliberately instead of running a repeating permission prompt sequence as though the status guaranteed another dialog.

teaching_blocks.title: Apply it to the supplied feature
teaching_blocks.content: Branch on the request result. A denied result can reflect not-yet-requested or previously denied access; restricted means the OS limits access, such as through parental controls. Provide the specified unavailable-feature fallback rather than continuing as granted. For an appropriate permanentlyDenied result, offer `openAppSettings()` because the user must change permission in settings. On Android, the status getter reports denied even for permanent denial, so use the request result to distinguish that permanent-denial case.

teaching_blocks.title: Keep the distinction clear
teaching_blocks.content: Android's denied status getter is not enough to prove a fresh prompt is possible. Also, repeatedly requesting a permanently denied permission does not replace the needed system-settings change. Denied and OS-restricted access should not be treated as authorization.

Check that no protected feature action continues in the denied or restricted branches, while preserving the user's decision rather than inventing an automatic permission recovery.

teaching_blocks.title: The situation
teaching_blocks.content: A supplied feature keeps a simple display setting, a text document, and a collection of structured local records. Storage choice follows data shape and retrieval operations. These are contextual examples of the supplied mechanisms rather than an exhaustive taxonomy of all possible storage systems. Keep the preferences durability limitation beside the importance decision: an awaited setter does not guarantee durable persistence when it returns. If the proposed value is critical, do not let its small size alone justify preferences.

teaching_blocks.title: The situation
teaching_blocks.content: A supplied multi-operation persistence action must not report success if a required operation fails. teaching_blocks.title: The working contract
teaching_blocks.content: Await each persistence operation and report success only after it completes successfully. An exception thrown out of a transaction causes rollback; completing its callback without an exception commits the transaction. Do not suppress a persistence exception inside the transaction when rollback is required; propagate it to the boundary that translates failure for the caller. Use the transaction object for operations inside `db.transaction((txn) async { ... })`, rather than call the database object and deadlock. Catch expected SQL failures with `on DatabaseException catch (e)` at the persistence boundary and return or propagate the application-facing failure rather than report success.

teaching_blocks.title: Trace the relationships
teaching_blocks.content: Use exception propagation to predict the transaction result. If the callback completes without an exception, it commits; if an exception escapes, it rolls back. Catching a required failure inside the callback and suppressing it changes that prediction, so propagation is part of the operation's correctness. Within the transaction, use txn for operations rather than the database object, which can deadlock in this pattern. At the application-facing boundary, expected DatabaseException handling turns a persistence failure into the prescribed failure result. Trace each operation's awaited completion so a success message cannot precede an unfinished or failed required write.

teaching_blocks.title: The situation
teaching_blocks.content: A supplied app and its third-party SDKs collect or share data. Store disclosures must describe that actual inventory, not only the collection statements the learner wrote directly. A privacy policy and Data safety declarations should stay aligned with the shipped behavior.

teaching_blocks.title: The working contract
teaching_blocks.content: Publish an accessible privacy policy describing collected data, its uses, third-party sharing, retention, deletion, and consent withdrawal. Inventory data collected or shared by the application and its third-party SDKs rather than report only collection written directly in application code. Map that actual inventory to the Google Play Data safety declarations, including the relevant collection, sharing, security, and deletion information. Check privacy declarations against the shipped permission and telemetry behavior and update them when the implementation changes.

teaching_blocks.title: Trace the relationships
teaching_blocks.content: Map actual behavior into disclosures rather than mapping desired disclosures back into a fictional build. Include collection and sharing performed by third-party SDKs as well as application code. The policy covers the stated uses, sharing, retention, deletion, and consent withdrawal, while Data safety uses the inventory for its relevant collection/sharing/security/deletion declarations. Compare permission and telemetry implementation with those declarations, especially after a change. The exercise asks for fidelity to the shipped behavior, not new legal advice or invented SDK practices. Keep each supplied inventory item traceable to the applicable disclosure instead of assuming SDK data is outside the application's report.

teaching_blocks.title: Apply it to the supplied feature
teaching_blocks.content: Inventory application and SDK data collection/sharing. teaching_blocks.title: Keep the distinction clear
teaching_blocks.content: An SDK's collection is not excluded simply because application code did not perform it directly. Also, filling out a disclosure form once is not proof it still describes a changed implementation. The inventory and shipped behavior are the grounding inputs.

teaching_blocks.title: Check the result
teaching_blocks.content: Use a supplied data-flow inventory and release behavior to compare each applicable disclosure item. Identify discrepancies without inventing legal conclusions or additional data practices. Check policy accessibility and the stated coverage topics, then keep declarations synchronized with the implementation being submitted.

teaching_blocks.title: The situation
teaching_blocks.content: A supplied release journey must work for users and reviewers. Review readiness checks the real release build, required services, and access to gated functionality; successful local development is not the complete submission check.

teaching_blocks.title: The working contract
teaching_blocks.content: Review the release as an actual user-facing application and resolve crashes, bugs, broken links, and incomplete behavior before submission. Test its release build on the intended supported targets and verify that backend services required by the journey are live and accessible. Provide working review access, such as a demo account or supported demo mode, for account-gated functionality. On Google Play, resolve errors reported in the release review summary before publishing; warnings should also be addressed where possible.

teaching_blocks.title: Trace the relationships
teaching_blocks.content: Use the same release journey for the user-facing check and the reviewer-access check. The release build should work on its intended targets with live accessible backend services, and the reviewer should have working access to account-gated functionality. Then inspect Play's release review summary. Errors are resolved before publishing; warnings are addressed where possible, preserving that qualification. A successful startup, a nominal demo account, and an uploaded build are separate observations that do not replace completing the main flow. Record a concrete blocking failure when one exists rather than treating the presence of release artifacts as review readiness.

teaching_blocks.title: Keep the distinction clear
teaching_blocks.content: A working app launch does not prove its main journey or reviewer access works. Also, a gated feature cannot be meaningfully reviewed through an unusable demo account. Errors must be resolved, while the guidance for warnings is to address them where possible.

Preserve the distinction between errors and warnings rather than upgrading every warning into an absolute publishing rule.

teaching_blocks.title: The situation
teaching_blocks.content: A supplied store upload is part of submission, not necessarily the act that sends a release for review or publishes it. Track the store's state and next valid action so an uploaded build is not mistaken for an available release.

teaching_blocks.title: The working contract
teaching_blocks.content: Complete the release's required build, listing, app-content declarations, and release notes, then resolve blocking errors in the store review summary before submitting. Google Play Changes not yet sent for review means changes exist but have not been submitted; send those changes for review through Publishing overview rather than assume upload submitted them. In review means the store is reviewing the update, not that it has already been published. For App rejected or Update rejected, read the policy issue, correct it and resubmit, or use the supported appeal process. Choose the intended testing or production audience and verify the published status and availability; publication timing can be controlled through managed publishing on Google Play. Uploading an iOS build to App Store Connect first starts build processing; wait for processing to finish before selecting the build for its version and submission workflow.

teaching_blocks.title: Apply it to the supplied feature
teaching_blocks.content: Complete the required build, listing, app-content declarations, and release notes, then resolve blocking review-summary errors. For App rejected or Update rejected, read and correct the policy issue and resubmit, or use the supported appeal process. Select the intended testing or production audience and verify published status and availability; managed publishing can control timing. On iOS, wait for uploaded-build processing before selecting it for the version/submission workflow.

teaching_blocks.title: Keep the distinction clear
teaching_blocks.content: Upload, review, and publication are distinct states. A rejected update is not an already-published success, and an iOS upload must finish processing before the build-selection step.

teaching_blocks.title: Keep the scope focused
teaching_blocks.content: Read the supplied current state and identify its next permitted action without inventing a processing or review duration.
